1.summary: God, who spoke through the prophets, has now spoken by his Son, heir of all things, through whom he made the world, who radiates his glory, sustains all things and, having made purification for sins, sat down at God's right hand; a chain of Old Testament quotations shows the Son is far above the angels.
1.lookfor: Notice the seven things said about the Son in verses 2 and 3, and the string of quotations that follows.

insights.title: A sermon, not a letter
insights.body: Hebrews has no greeting; it begins like a sermon. Its Greek is the most polished in the New Testament, with rolling sentences and careful rhythm.

insights.title: Spoken by his Son
insights.body: God spoke long ago in many ways through the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (1:1-2). The prophets were partial; the Son is God's final word.

insights.title: Radiance and exact imprint
insights.body: The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his being (1:3). The word charaktēr meant the stamp on a coin: Jesus bears God's exact likeness.

insights.title: He sat down
insights.body: Having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (1:3). Priests never sat down while serving; a seated priest means the work is finished.

insights.title: Why angels?
insights.body: Some Jewish teaching held that angels delivered the law at Sinai, and some honored them highly. If the Son is greater than angels, his message is greater than the law.

insights.title: You are my Son
insights.body: The writer strings seven quotations from the Psalms and 2 Samuel, including you are my Son and your throne, O God, is forever (1:5, 1:8). Royal psalms find their full meaning in Jesus.

insights.title: God's final word
insights.body: Hebrews says God's clearest word is a person, his Son. When you want to know what God is like, where do you look first?

2.summary: The writer warns not to drift from so great a salvation; though for a little while made lower than the angels, Jesus was crowned with glory, tasted death for everyone, and became like his brothers in every way, so he could be a merciful high priest and destroy the devil's power over death.
2.lookfor: Notice the first warning passage, and why Jesus had to become fully human.

insights.title: Drift
insights.body: We must pay closer attention to what we have heard, so we don't drift away (2:1). The word pictures a boat slipping past its harbor, not a dramatic rebellion but a slow drift.

insights.title: What is man?
insights.body: The writer quotes Psalm 8: what is man, that you think of him? You made him a little lower than the angels and crowned him with glory (2:6-7). We don't yet see everything subject to humanity, but we see Jesus (2:8-9).

insights.title: Pioneer
insights.body: It was fitting to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings (2:10). The word archēgos means pioneer or trailblazer, one who goes ahead and opens the way.

insights.title: Not ashamed to call them brothers
insights.body: He is not ashamed to call them brothers (2:11), quoting Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross.

insights.title: Why he became human
insights.body: Since the children share flesh and blood, he shared it too, so that by death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, the devil, and free those enslaved by fear of death (2:14-15).

insights.title: A merciful high priest
insights.body: He had to be made like his brothers in every way, to be a merciful and faithful high priest (2:17). Because he suffered when tempted, he can help those who are tempted (2:18).

insights.title: Drifting
insights.body: Drifting happens slowly and quietly. Where might you be drifting from Christ without noticing?

3.summary: Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, as a builder is greater than the house and a son greater than a servant; the writer warns, using Psalm 95, against hardening hearts like the wilderness generation who did not enter God's rest because of unbelief.
3.lookfor: Notice the repeated word "today" and the call to encourage one another daily.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: Faithful servant in God's house.

insights.title: Consider Jesus
insights.body: Consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus (3:1). He is both God's messenger to us and our representative to God.

insights.title: Faithful in all his house
insights.body: Moses was faithful in all God's house as a servant (3:5), as God said in Numbers. Jesus is faithful over the house as a son (3:6).

insights.title: Why compare with Moses?
insights.body: For Jewish readers, Moses was the greatest figure in history, the one who spoke with God face to face. To go back to Moses' system would be to choose the servant over the Son.

insights.title: Today, if you hear his voice
insights.body: The writer quotes Psalm 95: today, if you hear his voice, don't harden your hearts as in the rebellion (3:7-8), recalling Israel's testing of God at Meribah and Massah.

insights.title: Today
insights.body: Exhort one another every day, as long as it is called today (3:13). Today is the window of opportunity, and it stays open now.

insights.title: Because of unbelief
insights.body: The wilderness generation couldn't enter because of unbelief (3:19). They had been rescued from Egypt yet failed to trust God for the next step.

insights.title: Daily encouragement
insights.body: The writer says sin's deceitfulness is countered by daily encouragement from others. Who encourages you, and whom do you encourage?

4.summary: God's promise of rest still stands, since Joshua didn't give the final rest; a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, so they should strive to enter it; God's word is living and sharp, and with Jesus as a sympathetic high priest we can approach the throne of grace with confidence.
4.lookfor: Notice the three kinds of rest, and the invitation at the end.

names.name: Joshua
names.gloss: Moses' successor, who led Israel into Canaan.

names.name: David
names.gloss: The king through whom God spoke Psalm 95.

insights.title: Three rests
insights.body: God rested on the seventh day; Joshua led Israel into the rest of Canaan; yet David, long after, still spoke of today (4:4-8). So a greater rest remains.

insights.title: A Sabbath rest
insights.body: There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (4:9). The word sabbatismos appears only here: the full rest of God's new creation, which faith enters now.

insights.title: Strive to rest
insights.body: Let us labor to enter into that rest (4:11). A paradox: the effort is to keep trusting, not to earn.

insights.title: Sharper than a sword
insights.body: God's word is living, active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing soul and spirit, joints and marrow (4:12). The image is of a sacrifice laid open; nothing is hidden from him.

insights.title: Tempted in every way
insights.body: We don't have a high priest who can't sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every way like us, yet without sin (4:15).

insights.title: The throne of grace
insights.body: Let us draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (4:16). In the temple only the high priest could approach God's throne; now every believer can.

insights.title: Help in time of need
insights.body: You are invited to come boldly for help when you need it. What do you need to bring to God's throne of grace today?

5.summary: Every high priest is chosen from among men to offer sacrifices and must be called by God, as Aaron was; Christ was appointed by God a priest after the order of Melchizedek, learned obedience through suffering and became the source of salvation; the writer rebukes readers for being slow learners who still need milk.
5.lookfor: Notice the description of Jesus' prayers in verse 7, and the sharp rebuke at the end.

names.name: Aaron
names.gloss: Moses' brother, Israel's first high priest.

names.name: Melchizedek
names.gloss: A mysterious priest-king who blessed Abraham.

insights.title: A high priest's job
insights.body: Every high priest is taken from among men and appointed to act for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins (5:1). He could deal gently with the ignorant because he too was weak (5:2).

insights.title: Called, not self-appointed
insights.body: No one takes this honor for himself; he must be called by God, as Aaron was (5:4). Christ, too, didn't glorify himself (5:5).

insights.title: After the order of Melchizedek
insights.body: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (5:6), from Psalm 110, the most quoted psalm in the New Testament. Jesus, from Judah, couldn't be a Levitical priest, but this older priesthood fits him.

insights.title: Loud cries and tears
insights.body: In the days of his flesh, he offered prayers with loud cries and tears to the one able to save him from death, and was heard (5:7). Most readers see Gethsemane here.

insights.title: Learned obedience
insights.body: Though he was a Son, he learned obedience by the things he suffered (5:8). Not that he was disobedient, but he learned by experience what obedience costs.

insights.title: Milk and solid food
insights.body: You need milk, not solid food (5:12). Mature believers have trained their senses by practice to distinguish good from evil (5:14). Growth comes by use, like an athlete's training.

insights.title: Growing up
insights.body: The writer says they should be teachers by now. What would it look like for you to take the next step in spiritual maturity?

6.summary: The writer urges readers to go on to maturity, warns solemnly that those who fall away after tasting God's gifts cannot be restored, yet is confident of better things for them; God's promise to Abraham, confirmed by an oath, is an anchor for the soul, reaching behind the curtain where Jesus has gone.
6.lookfor: Notice the hard warning and the comfort that follows it, and the anchor image.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: Who patiently waited and received the promise.

names.name: Melchizedek
names.gloss: The priest-king whose order Jesus belongs to.

insights.title: Beyond the basics
insights.body: Let's move on from the elementary teaching: repentance, faith, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment (6:1-2). Foundations matter, but you don't keep relaying them.

insights.title: A hard warning
insights.body: It's impossible to restore again to repentance those who were enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift, and then fell away (6:4-6). Christians debate whether this describes true believers or those who only came close; all agree it is a serious warning against turning away.

insights.title: Land and thorns
insights.body: Land that drinks the rain and bears useful crops is blessed; land that bears thorns is near to being cursed (6:7-8), echoing Isaiah's song of the vineyard.

insights.title: Better things
insights.body: Even though we speak like this, we are confident of better things concerning you (6:9). God won't forget their love and service (6:10). The warning is meant to keep them going, not to crush them.

insights.title: God's oath
insights.body: People swear by someone greater; God, having no one greater, swore by himself (6:13). Two unchangeable things, his promise and his oath, give us strong encouragement (6:18).

insights.title: An anchor behind the curtain
insights.body: This hope is an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, entering within the curtain, where Jesus went as our forerunner (6:19-20). The anchor is fixed not on the sea floor but in God's presence.

insights.title: Anchored
insights.body: Hope in Christ is described as an anchor in a storm. What storm are you in, and what holds you steady?

7.summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, without recorded genealogy, blessed Abraham and received his tithe, showing his superiority to Levi; since the Levitical priesthood couldn't bring perfection, God appointed by oath a new priest forever, Jesus, who always lives to intercede for us.
7.lookfor: Notice the argument from what Genesis doesn't say about Melchizedek, and the contrast between many priests who die and one who lives forever.

names.name: Melchizedek
names.gloss: King of Salem and priest of God Most High.

names.name: Salem
names.gloss: An early name for Jerusalem; it means peace.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: Who gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils.

names.name: Levi
names.gloss: Ancestor of Israel's priestly tribe.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: The royal tribe from which Jesus came.

insights.title: King of righteousness and peace
insights.body: Melchizedek means king of righteousness, and king of Salem means king of peace (7:2). His very titles point to the Messiah.

insights.title: Without genealogy
insights.body: Without father, mother or genealogy, with no beginning of days or end of life (7:3). Genesis records none of these for him, unusual for a priest, whose lineage was essential. The writer reads the silence as a picture of an eternal priesthood.

insights.title: In Abraham's loins
insights.body: Levi, so to speak, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in his ancestor's body (7:9-10). So Melchizedek's priesthood outranks Levi's.

insights.title: Why a new priesthood?
insights.body: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why would another priest be needed? (7:11). A change of priesthood means a change of law (7:12).

insights.title: Sworn by oath
insights.body: Levitical priests became priests without an oath, but Jesus with one: the Lord has sworn and won't change his mind (7:20-21), from Psalm 110.

insights.title: He always lives to intercede
insights.body: He is able to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (7:25). One priest, one sacrifice, praying forever.

insights.title: He prays for you
insights.body: Hebrews says Jesus always lives to intercede for his people. How does it change your day to know Jesus is praying for you?

8.summary: Our high priest serves in the true tabernacle in heaven, of which the earthly one was a copy and shadow; he mediates a better covenant on better promises, the new covenant foretold by Jeremiah, which makes the first one obsolete.
8.lookfor: Notice the copy-and-reality contrast, and the long quotation from Jeremiah.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: Who was shown the heavenly pattern for the tabernacle.

names.name: Israel
names.gloss: God's covenant people.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: The southern kingdom, named in the new covenant promise.

insights.title: The main point
insights.body: The writer sums up: we have such a high priest, seated at the right hand of the throne, a minister in the true tabernacle the Lord pitched, not man (8:1-2).

insights.title: According to the pattern
insights.body: Moses was warned to make everything according to the pattern shown on the mountain (8:5). The earthly tabernacle was a copy and shadow of the heavenly reality.

insights.title: Better
insights.body: Better is a key word in Hebrews: a better covenant, better promises (8:6), better hope, better sacrifices. It appears about thirteen times.

insights.title: The new covenant
insights.body: The writer quotes Jeremiah's new covenant in full (8:8-12): laws written on hearts, everyone knowing God, sins remembered no more. It's the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament.

insights.title: Fault with the first
insights.body: If the first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no need for a second (8:7). The fault lay with the people (8:8), whose hearts the old covenant couldn't change.

insights.title: Ready to vanish
insights.body: By calling it new, God made the first obsolete, and what is growing old is ready to vanish away (8:13). If written before AD 70, the temple's fall was only a few years off.

insights.title: Written on the heart
insights.body: The new covenant promises God's law written on our hearts. Where do you see God changing your desires, not just your behavior?

9.summary: The writer describes the earthly tabernacle and its rituals, where the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood, unable to cleanse the conscience; Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary once for all with his own blood, securing eternal redemption, and will appear a second time to save those who wait for him.
9.lookfor: Notice the description of the tabernacle's furniture, and the repeated phrase once for all.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: Who sprinkled blood to inaugurate the first covenant.

insights.title: The tabernacle's layout
insights.body: The tent had two rooms: the Holy Place with lampstand, table and bread, and the Most Holy Place with the ark containing the manna jar, Aaron's rod and the tablets (9:2-4).

insights.title: Once a year
insights.body: Only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, not without blood (9:7), on the Day of Atonement. The way into God's presence was not yet open.

insights.title: The conscience
insights.body: Gifts and sacrifices couldn't make the worshiper perfect in conscience (9:9). Christ's blood cleanses the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (9:14).

insights.title: Testament
insights.body: The Greek word diathēkē means both covenant and will. A will takes effect only after a death (9:16-17), so Christ's death puts the new covenant into force.

insights.title: No forgiveness without blood
insights.body: Without shedding of blood there is no remission (9:22). The law taught that life is in the blood, given on the altar for atonement.

insights.title: Once for all
insights.body: Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by his sacrifice (9:26). As people die once and then face judgment, Christ was offered once and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save (9:27-28).

insights.title: A clean conscience
insights.body: The writer says Christ's blood cleanses the conscience. Is there something you still carry guilt for that Christ has already dealt with?

10.summary: The law's repeated sacrifices could never take away sins, but by Jesus' single offering of his body, he has perfected forever those being sanctified; so we may draw near with confidence, hold fast, meet together and encourage one another, remembering how they endured persecution and that God's coming one will not delay.
10.lookfor: Notice the contrast between standing priests and the seated Christ, and the three "let us" invitations.

insights.title: Reminder, not removal
insights.body: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, for the blood of bulls and goats can't take sins away (10:3-4). They pointed beyond themselves.

insights.title: A body you prepared
insights.body: The writer hears Christ speaking Psalm 40: sacrifice you didn't desire, but a body you prepared for me; I have come to do your will (10:5-7). Obedience in a human body is the true sacrifice.

insights.title: Standing and sitting
insights.body: Every priest stands daily offering the same sacrifices; but Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at God's right hand (10:11-12).

insights.title: Through the curtain
insights.body: We have boldness to enter the holy place by Jesus' blood, by a new and living way through the curtain, that is, his flesh (10:19-20). The Gospels tell of the temple curtain torn at his death.

insights.title: Let us
insights.body: Let us draw near; let us hold fast our hope; let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not giving up meeting together (10:22-25). Faith, hope and love in three invitations.

insights.title: Joyfully accepting loss
insights.body: The readers had once endured public insults and joyfully accepted the seizure of their property, knowing they had a better possession (10:32-34). The writer calls them to remember their own courage.

insights.title: Don't throw away your confidence
insights.body: Don't throw away your confidence, which has great reward (10:35). The word is parrēsia, boldness: the free access and courage that faith brings.

insights.title: Meeting together
insights.body: Some had stopped meeting with other believers. What helps you keep showing up, and whom could you stir up to love?

11.summary: Faith is the assurance of things hoped for; the writer traces it through Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab and many others, who trusted God's promises without receiving them in their lifetimes, some winning victories and others enduring torture.
11.lookfor: Notice how each person acts "by faith," and how the list moves from triumph to suffering.

names.name: Abel
names.gloss: Adam's son, whose offering God accepted.

names.name: Enoch
names.gloss: Who walked with God and was taken without dying.

names.name: Noah
names.gloss: Who built the ark.

names.name: Sarah
names.gloss: Abraham's wife, who bore a son in old age.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Jacob's son, who gave instructions about his bones.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: The prostitute of Jericho who welcomed the spies.

names.name: Gideon
names.gloss: A judge who defeated Midian with 300 men.

names.name: Samson
names.gloss: A judge of great strength.

insights.title: Assurance
insights.body: Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen (11:1). The word hypostasis could mean a title deed: faith holds the guarantee of what's promised.

insights.title: Pleasing God
insights.body: Without faith it's impossible to please God; whoever comes to him must believe he exists and rewards those who seek him (11:6).

insights.title: Abraham and Isaac
insights.body: Abraham offered Isaac, reasoning that God could raise him from the dead, and figuratively received him back (11:17-19).

insights.title: Strangers and pilgrims
insights.body: They confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, seeking a homeland, a heavenly one (11:13-16). The patriarchs lived in tents in a land promised but not possessed.

insights.title: Rahab in the list
insights.body: Rahab the prostitute, a Canaanite, stands in the same list as Abraham and Moses (11:31). Faith, not pedigree, places her there, and Matthew names her in Jesus' family tree.

insights.title: Victory and suffering
insights.body: Some through faith conquered kingdoms and shut lions' mouths; others were tortured, sawn in two, went about in sheepskins (11:33-37). Faith doesn't always look like winning. A Jewish tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two.

insights.title: Not without us
insights.body: None of them received what was promised, since God had something better, so that apart from us they shouldn't be made perfect (11:39-40). Their story and ours are one story.

insights.title: Your line in the list
insights.body: Each of these people acted on God's promise without seeing it fulfilled. What step of faith is God asking you to take before you can see the outcome?

12.summary: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, we run with endurance, looking to Jesus; hardship is the Father's loving discipline; the writer urges peace, holiness and grace, warns by Esau's example, and contrasts Mount Sinai's terror with Mount Zion's joyful assembly, calling for reverent worship of God, a consuming fire.
12.lookfor: Notice the running image, the father's discipline, and the two mountains.

names.name: Esau
names.gloss: Jacob's brother, who sold his birthright for a meal.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: The mountain of God's city, the heavenly Jerusalem.

names.name: Abel
names.gloss: Whose blood cried out from the ground.

insights.title: A cloud of witnesses
insights.body: We are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses (12:1), the heroes of chapter 11, like spectators filling a stadium. Runners stripped off every weight to race.

insights.title: Looking to Jesus
insights.body: Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising its shame (12:2). He ran the race first and finished it.

insights.title: The Lord disciplines those he loves
insights.body: The writer quotes Proverbs: my son, don't despise the Lord's discipline, for whom the Lord loves he disciplines (12:5-6). Hardship can be training from a loving Father.

insights.title: A root of bitterness
insights.body: See that no root of bitterness springs up to trouble you and defile many (12:15), echoing Moses' warning in Deuteronomy.

insights.title: Esau
insights.body: Esau sold his birthright for one meal and later couldn't undo it, though he sought it with tears (12:16-17). Trading the eternal for the immediate.

insights.title: Two mountains
insights.body: You haven't come to Sinai, with fire, darkness and terror, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, angels, the church of the firstborn, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel's (12:18-24).

insights.title: A consuming fire
insights.body: Our God is a consuming fire (12:29), quoting Deuteronomy. Grace doesn't make God less holy; it brings us safely near the fire.

insights.title: What weighs you down
insights.body: The writer says to lay aside every weight and the sin that clings. What is slowing your race right now?

13.summary: The writer closes with practical commands: keep loving one another, show hospitality, remember prisoners, honor marriage, be content, remember leaders, go to Jesus outside the camp bearing his reproach, offer a sacrifice of praise and good works, and receives a blessing from the God of peace who raised Jesus, the great shepherd.
13.lookfor: Notice the variety of everyday commands, and the beautiful closing blessing.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: Paul's co-worker, recently released.

insights.title: Angels unawares
insights.body: Don't forget hospitality, for by it some have entertained angels without knowing it (13:2), as Abraham did with three visitors at Mamre.

insights.title: Never leave you
insights.body: Be content, for he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you (13:5), God's promise to Joshua, now spoken to every believer.

insights.title: The same yesterday, today and forever
insights.body: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever (13:8). Leaders change and die (13:7); he doesn't.

insights.title: Outside the camp
insights.body: The bodies of sin-offering animals were burned outside the camp; so Jesus suffered outside the city gate (13:11-12). Let us go to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach (13:13), leaving the comfort of the old system.

insights.title: A sacrifice of praise
insights.body: Offer a sacrifice of praise continually, the fruit of lips that confess his name, and don't neglect doing good and sharing (13:15-16). The animal sacrifices end; praise and generosity continue.

insights.title: The great shepherd
insights.body: May the God of peace, who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, equip you (13:20-21). Isaiah spoke of God bringing up the shepherd of his flock.

insights.title: Remember prisoners
insights.body: The writer says to remember prisoners as if in prison with them (13:3). Who is suffering out of sight whom you could remember in prayer or in practical help?

intro.who: The author doesn't give a name. Early guesses included Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and Priscilla; the third-century scholar Origen concluded that only God knows. The writer knew Timothy (13:23) and wrote polished Greek.
intro.when: Probably before AD 70, since it speaks of temple sacrifices as still going on (10:1-2), though some date it later.
intro.why: Written to believers, probably Jewish Christians, tempted under pressure to drift back from Christ. It calls itself a word of exhortation (13:22): a sermon showing that Jesus is greater than angels, Moses and the priesthood, that his one sacrifice fulfills the old covenant, and urging readers to hold fast.

outline.title: Greater than Moses; entering God's rest
The new covenant and the perfect sacrifice
